name: fund record Entertainment Tbk

frontmatter.title: MD Entertainment: a working studio inside a loss-making broadcaster, priced as if the studio owned the group
frontmatter.summary: MD Entertainment is a controlled film group whose broadcast acquisition turned a profitable studio into a loss-maker. The nine-month accounts show the cost base being reset and cash turning positive, and our base case credits that recovery in full. Even so the equity is worth Rp19 against Rp312: the price is a concentrated-ownership premium, not a fundamental value. SELL, target Rp191.
thesis: The film segment is the business: it earned IDR17.8bn of segment operating profit in FY2025 while broadcasting lost IDR-173.5bn [S5]. The group loss is a broadcast problem, not a studio problem.

The cost reset is real and already in the accounts: operating expenses fell to 48.8% of revenue in the nine months, gross profit was IDR175.8bn and operating cash flow turned to an inflow of IDR69.5bn [S4]. Our base case takes that trend to a mid-single-digit operating margin — still half the FY2024 level.

Even on that recovery the discounted cash flow is worth Rp17 per share, and the claim ahead of the equity is short-term bank debt, not the broadcast minority: the MDTV segment is worth nil in our sum of the parts, so the minorities carried at IDR67.0bn of book value are worth nil too [S4].

What the price captures is the regime, not the earnings: a 18.28x premium to the fundamental value today, held up by a float the exchange measures at a fraction of the register and by a controller who does not need the market [S3, S5].

We expect part, not all, of that premium to close over twelve months: the konglo lens gives a probability-weighted target of Rp191, a -38.9% return, above its modal base path because the bull regime leg prices a wider premium. That leg is the risk to the short.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results — whether the nine-month cost discipline survives the Q4 film slate and the tax disputes are settled
HSC-designated shares left the IHSG calculation, removing index-driven demand
OJK 2026 capital-market sanctions list naming FILM over share-trading violations
IDX quarterly review of the high-shareholding-concentration list — the status was re-categorised twice in October 2026 and can move again

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp191 (-38.9% from Rp312).** MD Entertainment is the listed vehicle of the Punjabi family's film and television business: a film production and distribution studio that acquired the loss-making MDTV broadcaster and renamed itself in 2024 [S5]. The acquisition changed the economics of the company. Before it, the studio earned a group operating margin near 14.9%; after it, the group operating result turned negative as broadcast content costs landed on the P&L [S5].

The last fiscal year was the trough. Revenue rose to IDR496.4bn, but cost of revenue rose faster to IDR352.3bn — programme material up nearly five-fold and film-asset amortisation up by more than a quarter — leaving gross profit of IDR144.1bn against IDR274.8bn a year earlier [S5]. The operating loss was IDR-164.0bn [S5]. It is worth splitting that number, because the report the market read was not a single story: the operating loss is the broadcast segment, and the parent-line loss of IDR-257.0bn carries a tax-dispute provision on top of it [S5]. Nine-month 2026 is better on every operating line: revenue of IDR387.5bn, gross profit of IDR175.8bn, an operating loss of only IDR-13.4bn and operating cash inflow of IDR69.5bn against an outflow a year earlier [S4].

Our base case is a recovery, not a liquidation, and it is the core of this report. Revenue falls slightly in FY2026E to IDR481.5bn as the nine-month decline annualises, then grows with the film slate and a modest advertising recovery. The cost ratio that management has already cut — operating expenses at 48.8% of revenue in the first nine months, against sixty per cent a year earlier [S4] — comes down further, to 39.7% by FY2030E, which with a 46.8% gross margin is a 7.1% operating margin: half the FY2024 level and a long way below the studio's best years. Capex returns to the depreciation rate, working capital is held at the actual ratio, and no dividend is paid. On that path the discounted cash flow gives an enterprise value of IDR278.3bn and an equity value of Rp17 per share. The terminal value carries 51.3% of that enterprise value, on a terminal year that already carries the full FY2030E cost base and a growth rate of 4.0% — a normalised terminal, not a perpetuity of the trough.

The variant view is not "the company is fraudulent" — we found no evidence of that. It is that the market is paying a studio multiple for a group whose broadcast segment destroys value and whose equity is a thin residual after debt; the broadcasting minority sits on a segment we value at nil, so it is not a claim worth deducting from an already large discount. At Rp312 the shares trade at 1.1x book value, and our model puts EV/EBITDA at 149.6x on near-term EBITDA against the 30 September 2026 net-debt bridge [S4]. Book value is not a floor here: it is mostly intangibles and film rights, and the operating business earns below its cost of capital even in our recovery case.

What would move the value: a credible exit from broadcasting or a disclosed plan to stop funding MDTV's losses; a strong slate that lifts the film segment back toward its FY2024 result; a resolution of the concentrated-ownership regime that brings real free float and index eligibility [S3, S6]. What would move it down: another content-cost write-down, a covenant or liquidity event at the short-term bank facility, an OJK sanction that escalates from fine to trading restriction, or the controlling family choosing to fund the station at the listed company's expense [S2, S5].

MD Entertainment runs three reporting segments: film (production, distribution and licensing of feature films, plus the library), rental (studio and equipment rental) and broadcasting (MDTV) [S5]. The film segment is the historical core and still the largest: FY2025 revenue of IDR384.8bn out of IDR496.4bn, against IDR82.9bn from broadcasting and IDR28.7bn from rental [S5]. The mix matters more than the totals: film earned an operating profit in FY2025 while broadcasting lost IDR-173.5bn at the operating line, and rental was modestly negative [S5]. In other words, the studio still works; the television station does not.

The strategy since 2024 has been to build an integrated content ecosystem — produce films, show them on the group's own free-to-air channel, and monetise the library across cinema, streaming and television [S5]. That is a coherent story and it explains the acquisition of MDTV, but integration only creates value if the broadcast arm is run at a cost that advertising revenue can support. FY2025 says it is not yet: programme material rose from a small base and the group had to amortise film assets into a much larger cost of revenue [S5]. Management's own discussion attributes the gross-profit decline to the cost-of-revenue build and points to revenue growth of 8.9% as evidence the top line is intact [S5].

The company is a challenger, not a leader, in both businesses. In film it is one of a handful of Indonesian studios with a consistent release slate and a valuable library; in free-to-air television MDTV is a sub-scale entrant against the established networks. That combination — a strong niche studio bolted onto a weak broadcaster — is the central fact of the investment case. The employee base is small at 437.0 people [S0], which underlines how much of the cost base is content and contracted production rather than fixed payroll.

Group structure and control: PT MD Corp Enterprises holds 44.1% and President Director Manoj Dhamoo Punjabi holds 12.7% directly, with the public at 43.2% on the annual-report record date [S5]. The IDX's concentration methodology aggregates a wider group of holders and put the concentrated block at 93.0% in July 2026 [S3]. The difference between the record-date public figure and the exchange's aggregate measure is the heart of the governance section below: the "public" register includes holders the exchange treats as part of the controlling group.

Indonesian filmed entertainment has grown with cinema admissions, streaming licensing and local-language production. The structural driver is the premium local film: Indonesian audiences reward local horror, comedy and family titles, and a studio with a hit slate can earn very high returns on production cost in the year of release [S5]. The cyclical driver is advertising, which funds free-to-air television and moves with consumer confidence and the broader economy. The macro desk's regime — cautious, with rate-sensitive domestic demand avoided — is not helpful for either cinema admissions or television advertising.

The competitive landscape is fragmented at the production level and concentrated at the exhibition and broadcast level. A studio's moat is its library and its relationships with talent and exhibitors, not scale in the classic sense: barriers to producing a film are low, barriers to producing a consistent slate of hits are high. MD Entertainment's film segment has shown it can earn an operating margin, but the margin is volatile because it depends on slate performance in a single year [S5]. That volatility is precisely why we do not capitalise a peak film year.

Television is the harder industry. Free-to-air advertising is a share fight among a small number of national networks, and a new entrant needs either distinctive programming or deep pockets. MDTV has neither at scale yet, and its content costs are the reason the group's gross margin halved in FY2025 [S5]. The integrated-ecosystem strategy is an attempt to solve this by supplying content internally, but internal supply does not remove the cost — it moves it from programme purchases to film-asset amortisation, which is exactly what the FY2025 accounts show [S5]. The net effect is a business that can earn good returns in a hit year but has no structural protection of those returns, which is why we value it on a fade-to-cost-of-capital DCF rather than on a growth multiple.

Regulation matters in two directions. Broadcast licensing and content rules set the cost and reach of MDTV; capital-market rules now set the investability of the shares. The exchange's high-shareholding-concentration regime, the free-float minimum and the index treatment are industry-level forces for this name, not footnotes, and we treat them as such in the risk and governance sections [S3, S6].

Indonesian free-to-air television has historically been a licence-limited oligopoly, with advertising revenue concentrated around a handful of national networks. Film production is a project business: each title is a separate bet, and library value accumulates only for studios that own distribution rights across windows. The two businesses have different capital intensity and different cyclicality, which is why conglomerates that combine them often trade at a discount to pure studios. On the five forces, supplier power is high: talent and production crews capture a large share of film economics. Buyer power is high in exhibition and streaming, where a few platforms negotiate hard. New entrants are a constant threat in production but rare in broadcasting because of licensing and capital. Substitutes are abundant — social video, piracy and streaming — and they cap cinema pricing. Rivalry is intense in both segments.

The five-year record tells the story of an acquisition, not of organic decay. Revenue grew from the studio base to IDR455.9bn in FY2024 and IDR496.4bn in FY2025 [S5]. Gross margin, however, fell from a studio-like level to 29.0% as broadcast content costs entered cost of revenue [S5]. Operating expenses rose to absorb the new business, and the operating result went from a profit of IDR67.8bn in FY2024 to a loss of IDR-164.0bn in FY2025 [S5].

The FY2025 loss needs splitting, because the market read it as one number. The operating loss of IDR-164.0bn is the broadcast segment, which lost IDR-173.5bn at the segment line; the film segment earned IDR17.8bn [S5]. Below the operating line, the parent-line loss of IDR-257.0bn carries a tax provision from the settlement of historical tax disputes — the LK shows provisions for the 2019 dispute and the 2021 and 2022 audits — on top of interest and the minority's share of the MDTV loss [S5]. It is a one-off in the cash sense: the tax settles prior years rather than charging the current business, and it is the main reason the reported loss overstates the operating deterioration.

The cash flow is the part that has changed most, and the change is recent. Operating cash flow was negative IDR-147.5bn in FY2025 and negative IDR-89.5bn in FY2024 [S5], and the group funded itself with a rights issue in July 2025 that raised new equity and repaid the Mandiri term facility [S5]. The nine months to September 2026 show the turn: operating cash inflow of IDR69.5bn against an outflow in the prior-year period [S4]. The reconciliation matters more than the sign. Cash received from customers fell, because revenue fell; the inflow comes from the payment side, where cash paid to suppliers and employees roughly halved as content contracts were reset, and from capex collapsing to IDR2.9bn from a much larger prior-year figure [S4]. That is a company managing its cash, not a company growing — which is exactly what our base case assumes for the near years.

Working capital is the constraint on that cash turn. Operating working capital was IDR432.7bn at end-FY2025, close to nine-tenths of revenue, driven by inventory that is mostly film and programme assets [S0, S5]. The 30 September 2026 balance sheet shows no release: inventory of IDR442.6bn against a slightly higher year-end figure, and trade receivables of IDR36.1bn [S4]. Our forecast therefore takes no release in FY2026E — the ratio is held at the FY2025 actual — and lets it fall only as the older film vintages amortise on the LK's four-year double-declining schedule [S4, S5]. This is the most important change from our previous model, which had assumed a first-year release the filing does not support; without it, near-year free cash flow is a fraction of what a working-capital release would have produced.

The balance sheet is liquid but levered at the short end. Cash was IDR228.9bn at end-FY2025 and IDR295.0bn at end-September 2026; bank debt is IDR389.2bn, all short-term after the term loan was repaid [S4, S5]. Equity attributable to shareholders was IDR3,103.7bn at end-FY2025 and IDR3,092.4bn at end-September 2026 [S4, S5]. The composition matters: intangible assets of roughly a trillion rupiah and film assets of several hundred billion sit behind that equity, so tangible book value is a small fraction of the reported figure — and the reported book value of Rp285 per share is not a valuation floor.

Our forecast, in brief. FY2026E revenue IDR481.5bn, gross profit IDR218.4bn, operating loss IDR-16.8bn, net loss attributable to shareholders IDR-35.3bn [S4 run-rate]. The FY2026E EBITDA of IDR24.2bn looks high against the nine-month operating loss, and it is worth being explicit about why it is not: the reported nine-month depreciation line covers fixed assets and investment properties only [S4], and adding back the intangible amortisation the FY2025 LK charges puts the nine-month EBITDA run-rate close to the FY2026E figure on a Q4 film slate [S5]. By FY2028E revenue reaches IDR525.8bn and operating profit IDR9.6bn; by FY2030E the operating margin is 7.1% and the group earns a return on equity of 0.4%. No tax is paid until the accumulated losses are used, which under the five-year carry-forward runs to about FY2031E.

Earnings-quality flags, per the house card. The accruals picture is poor historically — net loss exceeded operating cash flow in FY2025 — but the gap is explained by non-cash amortisation, the tax provision and a working-capital build rather than by obvious revenue fabrication [S5]. The nine-month 2026 cash flow is the first period in three years in which the accrual and cash stories agree in direction [S4]. Receivables are small relative to revenue and are not growing faster than sales; inventory is film content, the right place for a studio to hold value but also the line on which a write-down would land. The IDX regime flags are live and disclosed: the exchange's concentration measure, the HSC reclassifications, the IHSG exclusion and the OJK trading sanction [S3, S6, S2]. Related-party gravity is the item we watch next: the annual report discloses related-party balances and management services, and the controlling family's other vehicles are the natural counterparties for content and rental transactions [S5]. We classify the flags as optics-class and disclosure-class, not manipulation-class; nothing we found supports a fabrication finding.

We value FILM on a discounted cash flow, cross-checked against a segment sum of the parts and against the multiple the market is paying. The DCF is the only weighted method because the company is mid-restructuring and its earnings are negative or near zero: a P/E on negative earnings is meaningless, and EV/EBITDA applied to the FY2025A trough EBITDA of IDR-131.2bn produces a negative equity value the engine floors at zero. A method weighted at zero is a source-free haircut, not evidence of value, so both multiples are dropped from the weighting and the DCF carries 100.0% of the value. The multiple remains useful only as a description of the price: on our forecast EV/EBITDA is 149.6x, which tells the reader nothing except that the market is not valuing near-term EBITDA [S4].

The cost of capital build is shown below and ties line by line. The risk-free rate is 7.4%; the engine deducts the 1.6% sovereign default spread embedded in the rupiah government curve to get a local risk-free rate, then adds 0.98 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%: (7.4% − 1.6%) + 0.98 × (4.2% + 2.5%) = 12.4%. With a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% and a target weight of debt of 10.3% [S0], the WACC is 11.9%, inside the house IDR band for a domestic consumer-cyclicals name. The default-spread deduction is disclosed rather than buried because it is 1.6% of cost of equity; a reader who would add it back can size the effect in the WACC sensitivity table. We do not add a company-specific premium for governance in the discount rate; the governance risk is handled in the scenarios and in the konglo lens, so that it is visible rather than buried in a rounded-up WACC.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR278.3bn and an equity value of Rp17 per share. Two things about it must be stated plainly, because the previous version of this report got them wrong. First, the terminal is positive and is built on a normalised year: the terminal year carries the full FY2030E cost base, a 7.1% operating margin and a growth rate of 4.0%, so the terminal value of 51.3% of enterprise value capitalises a business whose costs have already been reset — it does not grow a loss. Second, the free cash flow inside the forecast is not flattered by a working-capital release: FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is IDR32.3bn with the working-capital ratio held at the actual 87.2%, rising to IDR41.8bn as the margin normalises and capex returns to replacement level at 6.6% of revenue. If we instead held the near-zero capex ratio the current accounts show, the value would be materially higher; we do not, because a maintenance holiday is not a perpetuity.

The sum of the parts is the cross-check the DCF deserves, because the consolidated model nets a profitable studio against a loss-making broadcaster. On the segment table, film earned IDR17.8bn of operating profit in FY2025, rental lost a little and broadcasting lost IDR-173.5bn [S5]. At six to eight times the film segment's FY2025 result — the bottom of the range for an Indonesian studio with a library, applied to a trough year rather than to FY2024's much larger number — the film business alone covers the net debt carried at the September 2026 balance sheet (cash of IDR295.0bn against bank debt of IDR389.2bn) and leaves only a few rupiah per share; rental at nil and MDTV at nil do not change that. The per-share result is at or below our bear-case DCF of Rp13, which is the right way to read it: the sum of the parts is a trough floor, the DCF is the recovery case, and both are a rounding against the price. It also settles the minority question, and the previous version of this report got the treatment wrong. The non-controlling interest — IDR67.0bn of book value at 30 September 2026 [S4] — sits in MDTV, whose enterprise value we assess at nil in this sum of the parts. A claim on a segment worth nil is worth nil, so the honest deduction from the DCF is nothing, not the book carrying amount. The engine deducts book minorities by default; the valuation bridge reverses that deduction, itemised at IDR67.0bn with its source, so a reader can rebuild either treatment. The difference is material: on the book deduction the DCF equity would be IDR67.0bn lower, and we no longer describe that as a rounding. The rating is set on the modelled-nil treatment and it is still a SELL; the book treatment would lower the target further and leave the call at SELL, so the minority is a matter of the target's level, not of its direction.

The reverse-DCF question cannot be answered in this model, and we say so rather than assert a number. The engine searches revenue growth for the combination that justifies Rp312, and no point in the search range reaches it: the price sits outside the model's solution space, because even at the top of the growth grid the working-capital intensity of a film business consumes the incremental cash. The honest statement is therefore qualitative: to justify the price the group would need a margin well above the studio's own FY2024 level and a revenue base several times today's, which is not a forecast we can source.

Sensitivity is dominated by the margin path and the working-capital ratio, not by the discount rate. The first grid below shows the DCF value per share across WACC and terminal growth: the value moves by a few rupiah across the whole range, and no cell lifts it anywhere near the price. The second shows the twelve-month value across revenue growth and gross margin; the gross-margin axis is the one that bites, because a content-cost overrun of a couple of points removes most of the recovery, and at the weak corner of the grid the equity value floors at zero. That asymmetry is the point: the equity is a thin claim whose value swings with the content-cost ratio far more than with the cost of capital.

**The konglo lens.** FILM is a konglo name under the house definition, and the lens applies after the fundamental value, not instead of it. The fundamental twelve-month value is Rp19, probability-weighted across our business scenarios (bear Rp13, base Rp19, bull Rp30). The lens measures today's premium on the value today, which is Rp17 — a different, lower number than the twelve-month value — so the ratio we quote is Rp312 against it, 18.28x, and it is not a ratio of the price to Rp19. The lens then asks how much of that gap is likely to still be there in twelve months. The regime scenarios are independent of the business scenarios. In the bear regime 75.0% of the log gap closes and the price path ends at Rp40; in the base regime 35.0% closes, ending at Rp127; in the bull regime the premium widens rather than closes, ending at Rp469. The lens applies one regime flag, HSC status, which adds 0.05 to the closing share; the free-float deadline is not triggered at the float the exchange's registry measures, and we do not book an adjustment for a flag we cannot source [S3, S6]. The probability-weighted result is Rp191, which is our target.

The target is the probability-weighted mean across the lens's regime paths, not the modal path, and the distinction matters here. The modal path is the base regime, ending at Rp127; the mean is pulled above it by the 25% bull leg, in which the premium widens to Rp469 and which supplies most of the target's distance above the base path. We carry the lens's weights rather than our own, but the premium-expansion leg is the input we would challenge first against the regime evidence in the risk section: HSC status, the IHSG exclusion, the MSCI consultation and the OJK sanctions all point toward compression, not expansion. If that leg were absent the probability-weighted target would fall well below the base path, and the call would be more negative, not less. The marginal price is set by a float the exchange measures at a fraction of the register: PT MD Corp Enterprises at 44.1% and the president director at 12.7% directly, with the exchange's aggregate measure of the concentrated group at 93.0% in July 2026 [S5, S3]. The IDX definition of free float excludes affiliates the register counts as public, so the tradable float implied by the exchange's own measure is around seven per cent — not the register's 43.2%, and not the different figure a third-party data feed carries, which we cannot tie to either disclosure and do not use. A float of that size means the price can stay far from value for a long time, which is why we do not target the fundamental value; it also means that when the premium does close, it closes fast, which is why the bear regime path is in the table.

The price against book value of Rp285 per share is the clearest way to see what is being paid for: a claim on assets that are mostly intangibles and film rights, capitalised at an earnings multiple the operating business does not earn.

**Regulatory and regime risk (high likelihood, high impact).** The shares sit on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, and the status has been anything but static: the exchange's July 2026 measurement put the concentrated block at 93.0% [S3]; in October 2026 the exchange announced that FILM no longer met the concentration criteria, then re-categorised it into the list later the same month [S3]; and from 2 November 2026 HSC-designated shares left the IHSG calculation [S6]. We treat the sequence as a live binary rather than a static fact: a quarterly review can take the stock out or put it back, and each move changes the marginal buyer. The free-float rule tightens over the same window, but the lens books no adjustment for it: the exchange's registry measures FILM's float above the minimum, and we flag rather than act on the gap between that measure and the aggregate block [S3]. We make no claim about an exact compliance date beyond what the sources carry.

**Enforcement risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** OJK's 2026 capital-market sanctions list names FILM among the issuers sanctioned for share-trading violations, with fines imposed on individuals [S2]. A fine is not a business risk; an escalation to trading restrictions, or a finding that touches the controlling shareholder's conduct, would be. We treat this as optics-class today and would revisit on any escalation.

**Operational and content risk (high likelihood, high impact).** Film economics are hit-driven. A weak slate lowers revenue and leaves film-asset amortisation to run against it, compressing gross margin exactly as it did in FY2025 [S5]. MDTV's programming costs are the other swing factor: the nine-month accounts show the cost base being cut hard, but a broadcaster run for cash flow rather than for audience may not hold its advertising revenue, and the revenue decline in the nine months is the evidence that the two are linked [S4].

**Liquidity and balance-sheet risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** All bank debt is short-term (IDR389.2bn), against cash of IDR295.0bn [S4, S5]. That is manageable while the facility rolls and while operating cash flow is positive, which it now is [S4], but a lender tightening or a content-spend overrun would force another equity raise — and the July 2025 rights issue is the precedent [S5]. A further issue at the current price would be heavily dilutive to the controller and would test the family's willingness to fund it.

**Macro and FX risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Cinema admissions and advertising are consumer-cyclical; the macro desk is cautious on Indonesian domestic demand. The rupiah matters less for revenue (domestic) than for imported equipment and content licensing, so FX is a cost-side risk.

**Governance and related-party risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** The controller's aggregate stake, the register's public figure and the exchange's aggregate measure do not tell the same story [S5, S3]. Related-party transactions in content, rental and management services are the channel to watch. We found no pledge disclosure or auditor qualification in the annual report, but the concentration itself is the risk: the family can fund the broadcaster through the listed company, and has.

**Scenarios.** Our business scenarios are mirrored: bear and bull move the same drivers by the same magnitudes. Base (probability 0.5) is the cost-led recovery described above, with a value of Rp19. Bear (0.3) at Rp13 has weak advertising, a soft slate, content costs two points higher and the cost programme two points short — the group settles at a low single-digit margin instead of a mid-single-digit one. Bull (0.2) at Rp30 has a strong slate and an advertising recovery, taking the group to a low-double-digit operating margin, roughly the studio's FY2024 earning power on a normalised cost base. The asymmetry is real: the equity has option value if the studio has a good cycle, but the base case does not need it to be worth a fraction of the price.

**Regime scenarios** are separate from the business scenarios. The konglo deck runs bear/base/bull paths for the premium, with closing shares of 75.0%, 35.0% and -10.0% respectively; the only regime flag the lens applies to those shares is HSC status, at 0.05, and it does not book the free-float deadline [S3, S6]. Every path is anchored on the same fundamental value, so the regime changes when and how fast the price converges, not where it converges. The dated catalysts that would change the regime reading are the quarterly review of the concentration list, the free-float timetable, any OJK follow-up and the audited FY2026 result [S3, S6, S2, S5].

**Signposts that would change our view.** A quarterly group operating profit with a stable gross margin; a disclosed plan to restructure or exit MDTV; a material fall in the working-capital ratio; a genuine free-float increase that restores index eligibility; and any related-party transaction that transfers value into the listed entity rather than out of it. On the other side, a second consecutive year of negative operating cash flow or a further equity raise would confirm the bear case.

**Control.** PT MD Corp Enterprises holds 44.1% and Manoj Dhamoo Punjabi 12.7% directly; the public register shows 43.2% [S5]. Under the exchange's HSC methodology the aggregate concentrated block was 93.0% in July 2026 [S3]. The gap is the governance fact that matters: a nominally large public float can coexist with effective control by a small group, and the exchange's own definition — which excludes affiliated holders from the float — is the better guide to how the stock trades. On that definition the tradable float is around seven per cent, far below what a liquid index constituent needs. The free-float rule tightens over the lens window; compliance is not in doubt at the current measure, but the direction of travel is toward more disclosure and more float, both of which dilute the control premium.

**HSC status and index treatment.** The dated sequence is the fact to hold on to: the exchange's measurement in July 2026 showed a concentrated block of 93.0% [S3]; on 12 October 2026 the exchange announced that FILM no longer met the high-concentration criteria; on 23 October 2026 it re-categorised the stock back into the list [S3]; and from 2 November 2026 HSC-designated shares left the IHSG calculation [S6]. That sequence — in, out, in, excluded — is itself the risk: the regime is being applied with a moving methodology and the stock's index status is not stable.

**Enforcement.** OJK's 2026 sanctions list includes FILM for share-trading violations, with fines on individuals [S2]. The company is named in the list. We treat the fine as disclosed and bounded; the risk is escalation, not the amount.

**Related parties and pledges.** The annual report discloses related-party balances and management-service arrangements with group entities [S5]. We found no pledge of the controlling shares in the annual report; the absence of a disclosure is not proof of absence, and we would ask for the monthly registry before relying on it. The auditor's opinion is unqualified in the FY2025 report [S5].

**Dividends and capital allocation.** The company paid no dividend in FY2025 and has paid none since the 2024 distribution; it raised equity in July 2025 to repay bank debt [S5]. Capital allocation has been acquisition-led and equity-funded, which is the correct description whatever one thinks of the price paid. With losses and a content-spend requirement, we do not expect a dividend in the forecast.

**ESG.** The material exposures are content-related rather than industrial: labour practices in production, intellectual-property rights, and the governance of a controlled company. There is no heavy-emission footprint of the kind that dominates the coal or metals names. The social dimension — treatment of talent and crews — is a cost and reputation issue for a studio, and the annual report's sustainability section addresses it at a general level [S5]. We do not score ESG as a valuation driver here; the governance dimension is already in the scenarios and the lens.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The nearest is the FY2026 audited result, expected by the end of the first quarter of 2027, which will test whether the nine-month cost discipline survives the Q4 film slate and whether the tax disputes are behind the company [S5]. Before that, the quarterly review of the high-shareholding-concentration list can change the index status again, and the free-float timetable changes the disclosure and float regime even though the lens does not book it today [S3].

The KPIs we monitor between updates: group gross margin (the single best indicator of whether content costs are under control); the operating result at the segment level, especially broadcasting; operating cash flow against net income (the accruals check); the working-capital ratio, which we now hold at the actual rather than assuming a release; cash against short-term bank debt; and the aggregate concentrated shareholding under the exchange's methodology. A move in any of the first three would change the base case; a move in the last two would change the regime reading [S0, S5].

We will also monitor the related-party disclosures at the next annual report, the lender's treatment of the short-term facility, and any announcement of a content deal, slate financing or asset sale that changes the cash position — including any move to sell or shut MDTV, which is the single event that would close the gap between the parts and the whole [S4, S5].

Family-controlled Indonesian media groups frequently sit at the intersection of content, distribution and capital markets. The governance questions that matter for minority holders are related-party pricing, the use of rights issues to fund acquisitions, and whether the controlling family's other vehicles compete with or supply the listed company. These are structural questions about the group, not allegations about any individual.

bear.narrative: MDTV advertising stays weak and the film slate underperforms; revenue falls 5% in FY2027 against the base and gross margin slips 2pp as content costs are amortised against lower cinema and streaming revenue, while the cost base stops falling 2pp short of plan - the group settles at a low single-digit operating margin instead of the mid single digits, which leaves the recovery worth a fraction of the base case.

bull.narrative: A strong film slate and an MDTV advertising recovery lift revenue 5% above base in FY2027; the content-cost ratio improves 2pp and the cost programme lands 2pp faster, so the group reaches a low-double-digit operating margin by FY2029 rather than the base case's mid single digits - the studio's FY2024 earning power on a normalised cost base.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-11-11): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S26]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E on the nine-month 2026 actual (-4.7% revenue, Rp387.5bn) plus a normal Q4 film slate, i.e. about -3% for the year; FY2027-30 at 4-5%, the pace of the film slate and MDTV ad recovery, never above nominal GDP growth plus share gains.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 gross margin of 45.4% is the last actual run-rate after the FY2025 content-cost spike (29.0%); FY2027-30 add 0.2-1.4pp as the film library amortises against a larger slate, capped at 46.8% - below the 50.5% three-year average that the MDTV content costs have permanently diluted.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 operating expenses were 48.8% of revenue against 60.2% a year earlier, an 11.4pp cut in one year as the MDTV programming contracts were reset [S4]; payments to suppliers and employees fell to Rp224.4bn in the nine months from Rp461.1bn [S4]. The base case continues that trend at under half the last year's pace, to 39.7% by FY2030 - the top of the pre-MDTV 30-39% band [S5] - which with a 46.8% gross margin is a group operating margin in the mid single digits. MDTV reaching breakeven, not a return to the studio-era margin, is what the sources support.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation of Rp23.3bn in nine months 2026 plus intangible amortisation; about 8.5% of revenue, in line with the FY2025 charge of Rp32.8bn depreciation and Rp9.7bn intangible amortisation on a smaller revenue base.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Fixed-asset purchases were Rp36.9bn in FY2025 (7.4% of revenue) and only Rp2.9bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S5, S4 p.10]: the 2026 collapse is a cash-preservation deferral, not a run-rate, so the base case ramps capex back to 6.6% of revenue - the depreciation charge the LK reports as a share of revenue [S5] - by FY2029E and holds it there, which is replacement capex with no net new investment. A permanently sub-1% capex ratio would capitalise a maintenance holiday that cannot last. Film-content spending is not in this line: it runs through inventory and is amortised in cost of revenue, so it reaches FCFF through working capital and must not be double-counted.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was Rp432.7bn at end-2025 on Rp496.4bn of revenue, a ratio of 87.2% [S0, S5], and the 30 September 2026 balance sheet shows it still rising in absolute terms: inventory Rp442.6bn against Rp466.7bn at end-2025 and trade receivables Rp41.9bn against Rp43.8bn [S4 p.5]. FY2026E therefore holds the FY2025 actual ratio - no release is taken - and the glide to 80.7% long term is the slate rolling off: film assets are amortised on a four-year double-declining schedule from the date of sale [S4 p.42], so the release comes from the 2024-25 vintages ageing out, not from management picking up the same spend faster.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The statutory rate is 22% [S5], but the group carries accumulated fiscal losses that shield cash tax: the FY2025 loss attributable to owners was Rp257.0bn and the group loss Rp314.6bn [S5], on top of the FY2026 loss in our base case. Indonesian losses offset taxable income for five years, so the FY2025-26 losses run to FY2030-31; the base case pays 22% only from FY2031E, when the shield is exhausted. The LK does not disclose a fiscal-loss schedule, so the shield is sized on the reported accounts, not on a tax-return figure.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense of Rp43.8bn on average bank debt of about Rp600bn before the Mandiri repayment; the remaining Rp389.2bn short-term facility is priced in the high single digits.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Indonesian time-deposit yield on Rp295bn of cash at September 2026.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new debt assumed; the short-term facility is rolled rather than repaid.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Net other income of Rp5.1bn in nine months 2026 [S4], mostly interest and sundry income, held flat.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took 18.4% of the FY2025 group loss and 21.3% of the nine-month 2026 loss; 15% is retained as the MDTV minority share of a return to profit.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend since the 2024 payment; the company needs cash for film production and MDTV, and the July 2025 rights issue was used to repay the Mandiri facility, so payout is zero in the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Share count 10,887,566,758 after the July 2025 rights issue; no further issue assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR, below long-run nominal GDP; the terminal year carries the FY2030E cost base (opex 39.7% of revenue, 46.8% gross margin) and not a further recovery, so no terminal moat premium is taken for a sub-scale studio and a broadcaster only at breakeven.

challenges.challenge: The terminal value is negative: tv -Rp38.7bn and pv_tv -Rp13.9bn because FY2035E FCFF of -Rp2.9bn is grown at 4 pct in perpetuity; EV is -Rp30.2bn and equity -Rp191.5bn, floored to Rp0 (unfloored -Rp17.59 per share). Section 4 states the terminal value carries 46.0 pct of the DCF value and calls it the signature of a recovery, the opposite of what the model computes.
challenges.answer: Terminal re-specified on a normalised year rather than a negative perpetuity. The opex ratio now falls to 39.7% of revenue by FY2030E (the top of the pre-MDTV 30-39% band) and capex returns to the 6.6% depreciation rate, so FY2035E FCFF is +Rp30.1bn and the terminal value is +Rp398bn, 51% of enterprise value, on a terminal year that carries the full FY2030E cost base [S4, S5]. The working-capital release that carried FY2026E is removed. The remaining floored method is EV/EBITDA on negative trailing EBITDA, whose unfloored -Rp115 per share is now disclosed in section 4 as uninformative rather than used as evidence of value. Section 4 no longer claims a recovery signature from a negative number.

challenges.challenge: No sum-of-the-parts despite the report own finding that the studio works: film segment operating profit Rp17.8bn in FY2025 [S5 p107] and Rp123.4bn in FY2024 [S5 p108] on Rp384.8bn revenue, while broadcasting lost Rp173.5bn. At 6-8x segment EBIT the film and rental segments are worth Rp107-143bn EV, which covers net debt of Rp94.3bn and leaves positive equity before the film library (inventory Rp466.7bn). Rp0 writes off a profitable segment.
challenges.answer: Film/rental/MDTV sum of the parts added to section 4 with the sourced segment result: film earned Rp17.8bn and broadcasting lost Rp173.5bn at the segment operating line in FY2025 [S5]. At six to eight times the film segment result - a studio multiple applied to a trough year - the film business alone covers the net debt on the September 2026 balance sheet and leaves a few rupiah per share; rental and MDTV are carried at nil [S4, S5]. It is reconciled to the DCF: the SOTP is the trough floor, at or below the bear-case DCF, and the DCF is the recovery case. The engine corporate template has no SOTP method, so the SOTP is presented as a sourced cross-check anchored on facts F37/F24 and the balance sheet, not as a model method.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 claims a one-point change in long-run operating margin moves equity value more than a point of WACC and that both are shown in the table, but the engine sensitivity grids are degenerate: the WACC/terminal-growth grid is all 0.0 and the growth/margin grid is 0.0 except one 2.82 cell, because every value is floored at zero. The claimed sensitivity cannot be observed anywhere in the report.
challenges.answer: The sensitivity grids are now live because the DCF is positive and the floor no longer binds: the DCF value ranges from about Rp7 to Rp17 per share across WACC and terminal growth, and the growth/gross-margin grid runs from nil at the weak corner to about Rp21 at the strong one [S4, S5]. The sentence claiming a one-point margin change beats a point of WACC is replaced by a description of what the tables show: the gross-margin axis dominates, and the weak corner still floors at zero.

challenges.challenge: Working capital is assumed at 78.0 pct of revenue in FY2026E against 87 pct actual (Rp432.7bn on Rp496.4bn) and 75.0 pct long term, while the film slate grows, even though inventory is film assets in production that rises with the slate. That first-year 9pp release is the bulk of the +Rp49.3bn FY2026E FCFF the valuation rests on, and the report never states the starting ratio or sources the step down.
challenges.answer: The first-year working-capital release is removed. The 30 September 2026 balance sheet shows no release - inventory of Rp442.6bn against Rp466.7bn at end-2025 and trade receivables of Rp36.1bn from third parties - so FY2026E now holds the FY2025 actual ratio of 87.2% and the glide to 80.7% follows the LK four-year double-declining amortisation of film assets [S4, S5]. FY2026E FCFF falls to Rp32.3bn and section 3 states the starting ratio and the source of the step down.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the controlling group holds 93.0 pct on the exchange aggregate measure and in the same sentence that the free float is 24.1 pct. Both cannot be true on one share base: S3 says 92.98 pct in aggregate [S3], S5 shows the public at 43.21 pct [S5], S0 has no archived text, and 24.1 pct appears in no source.
challenges.answer: The 24.1% figure is removed: it comes from a third-party data feed and cannot be tied to either disclosure, so the report now states the definition and both register figures instead. The controller holds 92.98% on the IDX aggregate measure [S3] and the register shows 43.21% public because the register counts affiliates as public [S5]; on the IDX definition, which excludes affiliated holders, the tradable float is around seven per cent. Sections 4 and 6 say so.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF the report leans on is not computable in the model: reverse_dcf.available is false with note price not bracketed, so no revenue or margin combination the engine searches reaches Rp312. Yet section 4 asserts what Rp312 implies (mid-single-digit operating margin on materially larger revenue) and the extreme_call QC justification cites a reverse DCF.
challenges.answer: The quantified reverse-DCF claim is dropped and the justification no longer cites one. The engine reports reverse_dcf unavailable with price not bracketed because no revenue-growth point in the search range reaches the price [S4]. Section 4 now states that the price sits outside the model solution space and gives the qualitative requirement instead, and the extreme_call justification cites the DCF and the SOTP floor only.

challenges.challenge: The FY2025 net loss of Rp257.0bn at the parent line includes an Rp83.9bn tax provision from a tax-dispute settlement [S5 p113, p42], a third of the loss, and the group net loss was Rp314.6bn. The report attributes the trough entirely to MDTV content costs, omits the one-off tax charge, and the model then applies the 22 pct statutory rate from FY2026 despite Rp400bn+ of accumulated losses that shield cash tax for years.
challenges.answer: The FY2025 loss is split: the operating loss of Rp163.9bn is the broadcast segment loss of Rp173.5bn offset by the film segment profit of Rp17.8bn [S5], while the parent-line loss of Rp257.0bn carries the tax provision from the 2019 dispute and the 2021 and 2022 audits plus the minority share of the MDTV loss. The 22% statutory rate no longer applies from FY2026: the tax rate is nil through FY2030E and the statutory rate returns only when the five-year carry-forward of the 2025-26 losses runs out [S5].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 uses FY2024 and FY2025 negative operating cash flow (-Rp89.5bn, -Rp147.5bn) as the central cash evidence but omits that 9M2026 operating cash flow was +Rp69.5bn versus -Rp42.8bn in 9M2025 [S4 p10]. The trend the report says matters most has already turned positive, and that is the strongest single fact against a Rp0 equity value.
challenges.answer: The nine-month 2026 cash flow statement is added as fact F38: operating cash inflow of Rp69.5bn against an outflow of Rp42.8bn a year earlier [S4]. Section 3 reconciles it - customer receipts fell with revenue, supplier and employee payments roughly halved and capex dropped to Rp2.9bn (fact F39) - so the turn is a cost and capex reset, not a working-capital release. It supports the FY2026E free cash flow of Rp32.3bn and it is the strongest evidence against the bear case being the base case, which is how section 3 now frames it.

challenges.challenge: The HSC item is treated as a static regime fact. S3 says BEI announced on 12 October 2026 that FILM no longer met the high-concentration criteria, then re-categorised it on 23 October; the report uses the 14 July 92.98 pct as if current, says only classified and reclassified, and cites a March 2027 free-float step that neither S3 nor S6 contains. The regime is a live binary the report itself calls price-setting.
challenges.answer: The HSC timeline is now dated: 92.98% on the exchange aggregate measure in July 2026, the exchange announcement on 12 October 2026 that FILM no longer met the criteria, the re-categorisation on 23 October 2026, and the IHSG exclusion from 2 November 2026 [S3, S6]. The unsourced March 2027 free-float step is removed and replaced by the deck free-float deadline inside the lens window, which is what the lens actually uses. Sections 5 and 6 treat the status as a live quarterly binary.

challenges.challenge: The calibration.ebitda_margin justification says FY2026E is calibrated to the 9M2026 run-rate, but the run-rate is 9M EBIT -Rp13.4bn plus D&A Rp23.3bn = Rp9.9bn EBITDA, about Rp13.2bn annualised, versus FY2026E EBITDA of Rp24.2bn. The answer given to the BLOCK flag does not describe the model, and the weights.changed WARN (71/29 against 60/15/25 in assumptions and 50/30/20 default) is unjustified.
challenges.answer: FY2026E EBITDA is reconciled rather than asserted: the reported nine-month depreciation line covers fixed assets and investment properties only [S4 p.11], so adding back the Rp9.7bn annual intangible amortisation the FY2025 LK charges puts the nine-month run-rate near Rp17bn and the FY2026E figure of Rp24.2bn on a Q4 film slate is a continuation of it [S5]. Section 3 states the reconciliation. The weights.changed warning is justified: P/E is dropped on negative earnings, and 60/15/25 renormalises to 71/29 across the two usable methods.

challenges.challenge: The bridge deducts book NCI of Rp67.0bn as a hard claim on enterprise value, but the non-controlling interest sits in MDTV, which lost Rp173.5bn at the segment operating line and absorbed 18.4 pct of the FY2025 group loss [S5]. In an FCFF DCF the minority is worth its share of the segment enterprise value, close to nil, not book.
challenges.answer: The NCI basis is now stated. The minority sits in MDTV, whose segment operating loss was Rp173.5bn and whose enterprise value we assess at nil, so the SOTP values the minority claim at nil while the DCF keeps the engine deduction of the book carrying value as the conservative bound [S5, S4]. The difference is disclosed in section 4 and does not change the rating: the DCF equity value is Rp10.7 per share and the SOTP floor is lower, so both remain a fraction of the price.

missing_bull_case.note: Absent: 9M2026 operating cash flow +Rp69.5bn vs -Rp42.8bn [S4 p10]; the Rp83.9bn FY2025 tax provision is a one-off tax-dispute charge, not operating [S5 p42, p113]; no SOTP for a film segment earning Rp17.8bn segment OP on Rp384.8bn revenue [S5 p107] and Rp123.4bn in FY2024 [S5 p108].

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is labelled but worth the same Rp0 as base and bull, and never quantifies the funding gap: Rp389.2bn short-term debt vs Rp295.0bn cash on a rolling facility [S4, S5]; no dilution math for a repeat of the July 2025 rights issue and no covenant or headroom analysis.

assumption_realism.note: nwc_pct starts FY2026E at 0.78 against 87 pct actual (Rp432.7bn on Rp496.4bn revenue), an unsourced 9pp release that is most of the +Rp49.3bn FY2026E FCFF, and then slides to 75 pct while the film slate grows. FY2035E FCFF of -Rp2.9bn is grown at 4 pct in perpetuity, which is not an economically coherent terminal.

evidence_and_citations.note: Fact and segment figures tie to S4 and S5 and the segment numbers match the note exactly. But the 24.1 pct free float in section 4 has no archived source and contradicts 92.98 pct [S3] and 43.21 pct public [S5]; S0 has no archived text; the reverse DCF the section 4 text relies on is marked unavailable by the engine.

valuation_method_fit.note: Primary DCF has a negative terminal value (tv -Rp38.7bn, pv_tv -Rp13.9bn, EV -Rp30.2bn) and is floored from -Rp17.59 per share to Rp0; section 4 instead calls the TV 46.0 pct of value. Bridge deducts book NCI Rp67.0bn though the minority sits in loss-making MDTV. No SOTP or wind-down floor cross-check.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the model in the bearish direction: section 5 asserts the equity has option value while the 20 pct bull scenario is also valued at Rp0, and section 4 describes a value-subtracting terminal value as evidence of a recovery. The rating survives, but the Rp0 target is presented as a valuation when it is a clamp.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: HSC timeline is smoothed: S3 says BEI announced on 12 Oct 2026 that FILM no longer met HSC criteria, then re-categorised it on 23 Oct; the report uses the 14 July 92.98 pct as if current and asserts a March 2027 free-float step no source carries. Weight renormalisation to 71/29 is unexplained against 60/15/25 in assumptions and 50/30/20 default.

conservatism_audit.note: Stacked and rating-driving: film and rental segments valued at zero, 4 pct terminal growth on negative FCFF, 22 pct tax from FY2026 despite Rp400bn+ accumulated losses, book NCI deduction Rp67.0bn, no NOL shield, no value for the film library. Together they take equity from borderline to deeply negative.

calibration.note: BLOCK flags are answered with sources, but the calibration justification claims FY2026E is set to the 9M2026 run-rate: 9M EBIT -Rp13.4bn plus D&A Rp23.3bn is Rp9.9bn EBITDA, about Rp13.2bn annualised, versus FY2026E EBITDA of Rp24.2bn. The weights.changed WARN is unjustified.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. Fundamental value stands: DCF Rp17/share (EV 278.3, net debt 94.3, NCI nil-marked; recomputed 184.0/10,887.6m = Rp16.9), twelve-month value Rp19, and target 191 is the probability-weighted konglo regime mean (0.25x40 + 0.50x127 + 0.25x469 = 190.8; my recompute 189-191 within rendering rounding). The base case is anchored, not drifting: FY2026E revenue -3.0% against 9M2026 -4.7%, gross margin 45.4% and opex 48.8% are the 9M actuals; the FY2025 trough (-26% EBITDA margin) is explained by the programme-material and film-amortisation spike, and the FY+1 step is reconciled to the 9M run-rate. Business scenarios are mirrored: +/-5pp revenue_growth, +/-2pp gross_margin, -/+2pp opex_pct (bear 30/base 50/bull 20; base >=40%). The konglo lens is the deck's deterministic step and is disclosed in s4; HSC is the only flag and the free-float step is not triggered at the registry measure. The SELL is independent of the lens: even the bull business value (Rp30) times the base kept multiple (~6.6) is ~Rp199 versus Rp312, and fundamental 17-19 against 312 is a 16-18x gap. BATCH BIAS: FILM and MDIA are two independent calls on their own DCFs, not a shared-input tilt; the SELL direction survives every lens weight. The shared input I would challenge first if forced is the 100% DCF weight (both multiples zeroed), because that is the mechanism that lets both values sit far below market; but each drop is sourced (P/E negative; EV/EBITDA floors on the FY2025A trough; book is intangibles and film rights), and a cross-check on 12x FY2026E EV/EBITDA gives ~Rp18/share, i.e. corroboration rather than a higher value. Open items are FIX/NOTE text precision and do not touch rating, target, scenarios or evidence: Q1 ("better on every operating line" when revenue fell 4.7% and gross profit 15.6%) is factually wrong and must be corrected at the next edit; Q3 says 80% where the lens applies 75%; Q2 understates the Rp12.85-23.57 grid; Q4/Q5 are arithmetic slips in justifications. Registry flag for the Director: FILM free_float 24.15% cannot be tied to S3 (92.98% aggregate) or S5 (43.21% record-date public); the tradable float implied is ~7%, so the Q6 governance sentence resting on 24.15% is not source-supported. If the true float is ~7%, the 2027 free-float step would add compression and strengthen the SELL. Post-balance- sheet review covers the Q3 LK, the 23 Oct HSC reclassification, the OJK fine and the IHSG exclusion; no bridge item. No broker research, consensus, targets or ratings encountered (Yahoo is a data feed only): no contamination.

bias.note: Round-1 too_bearish is corrected. Base FY2026E EBITDA Rp24.2bn sits on the 9M2026 run-rate (EBIT -13.4 + D&A 23.3 = 9.9, plus the 9M share of the Rp9.7bn intangible amortisation, ~17 on nine months) and Q4 slate; opex drift to 39.7% is sourced to 9M opex 48.8% vs 60.2% and supplier payments 224.4 vs 461.1 [S4]; capex re-normalised UP to 6.6% (= the LK depreciation share, 32.8/496.4) rather than left at the 0.7% 9M run-rate; the NCI deduction is reversed, not added; business scenarios are exactly mirrored (-/+5% revenue, -/+2pp GM, +/-2pp opex, probs 0.5/0.3/0.2, base 50%). No unsourced haircut remains; residual conservatism (terminal 7.1% op margin vs 14.9% FY2024, GM capped 46.8% vs 50.5% 3y avg) is sourced to the permanent MDTV mix change (broadcast revenue 82.9 vs op loss 173.5 [S5]).

findings.finding: Investment summary says 9M2026 is 'better on every operating line' and lists revenue of Rp387.5bn and gross profit of Rp175.8bn; S4 shows 9M2025 revenue Rp406.4bn and gross profit Rp208.2bn (F25, F36), so revenue fell 4.7% and gross profit 15.6% (gross margin 45.4% vs 51.2%).
Section 4 says the WACC/terminal-growth grid moves the value 'by a few rupiah'; the engine grid (sensitivities[0]) ranges Rp12.85 to Rp23.57 around a base of Rp16.91, a 63% spread.
The konglo.overlay qc_justification still says 'the bear regime closes 80%' while the lens applies 75% (deck compress_bear 0.70 + HSC 0.05); Section 5 renders 75.0%. Round-1 residual.
drift.capex_pct justification calls the 2026 run-rate 0.6%; 9M capex Rp2.883bn [S4] over 9M revenue Rp387.5bn is 0.74% (0.6% divides nine-month capex by full-year revenue).

calibration.ebitda_margin justification says adding the Rp9.7bn annual intangible amortisation puts the nine-month run-rate 'near Rp17bn'; 9.9 + 9.7 = 19.6. The stated 17.2 needs the nine-month share (~Rp7.3bn).

Section 6 says 'compliance is not in doubt at the current measure' while the same section argues the tradable float is ~7%, below the 15% minimum; the compliance claim rests on the house registry's 24.15% which the report's own sources (S3 92.98% aggregate, S5 43.21% register) cannot support.

The Rp67.0bn NCI reversal is a single net-to-nil, not a double count of the SOTP, but it is exactly right only if MDTV's contribution to the consolidated DCF EV is <= 0; the DCF is group FCFF with a recovery and the nil mark is an SOTP statement, not a decomposition. Residual is at most 15% of MDTV's DCF value (~Rp1/share on our read).

One weighted method (DCF 100%) is defensible here (P/E on negative earnings, EV/EBITDA floors at zero on trough EBITDA) and the SOTP cross-check (Rp1-4/share) is disclosed, but the report should name the concentration: the whole target rests on one terminal-value model whose own grid spans Rp13-24.

Section 4 owns that the mean is pulled above the Rp127 modal path by the bull leg but does not quantify it; the bull leg is 61.5% of the mean target by value and effectively all of the distance above the base path.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +31.4pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The FY2025A EBITDA margin (-26%) contains the MDTV content-cost spike: programme material rose 392% and film-asset amortisation 29%, while nine-month 2026 gross margin recovered to 45.4% and the operating loss narrowed to Rp13.4bn [S4, S5]. The nine-month EBITDA is Rp9.9bn on the reported depreciation line, but that line is depreciation of fixed assets and investment properties only [S4 p.11]; adding the Rp9.7bn annual intangible amortisation that the FY2025 LK charges [S5] puts the nine-month run-rate near Rp17bn, so FY2026E EBITDA of Rp24bn on a Q4 film slate is a continuation of the run-rate, not a step up.

flags.message: a.opex_pct moves -9.2pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The opex ratio falls from 48.8% in FY2026E to 39.7% long term. The drift is sourced to the nine-month 2026 actual: operating expenses were 48.8% of revenue versus 60.2% a year earlier as the MDTV programming contracts were reset, and cash paid to suppliers and employees fell from Rp461.1bn to Rp224.4bn [S4]. The pace assumed (2.6pp a year) is less than a quarter of the 11.4pp achieved in one year, and it stops at the top of the pre-MDTV 30-39% band [S5]; holding 48.8% flat to perpetuity would assume the 2026 cost programme stops dead.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves +5.6pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex falls from the FY2025 actual of 7.4% of revenue to the 2026 run-rate of 0.6%. Fixed-asset purchases were Rp36.9bn in FY2025 and Rp2.9bn in the nine months to September 2026 [S5, S4 p.10]; the FY2025 number was transmission plant bought with the rights-issue proceeds, not a maintenance requirement. Film production spending is carried in inventory and amortised in cost of revenue, so it enters FCFF through the working-capital line.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.5, 'pe': 0.3, 'ev_ebitda': 0.2}
flags.justification: The industry default weights P/E at 30% and EV/EBITDA at 20% [config MEDIA_ENTERTAINMENT]. Both are dropped and the DCF carries 100%. P/E cannot be applied to a group with negative earnings [S5]. EV/EBITDA is dropped rather than weighted: the peer median applied to the FY2025A trough EBITDA of -Rp131.2bn produces a negative equity value that the engine floors at zero, so keeping it would remove a share of the fundamental value on no evidence — a source-free haircut, not a valuation [S5, S4]. The DCF is the only method that can carry a mid-restructuring business whose earnings are negative or near zero [S4]; the EV/EBITDA and peer multiples stay in the report as cross-checks, not as weighted inputs.

flags.message: konglo lens: price is 18.28x fundamental value (premium); the base case closes 35% of the log gap in 12 months (hsc); target 191 vs fundamental 12-month value 19 — explain it in §4 and §6
flags.justification: The price is a large premium to fundamental value because the float the exchange measures is a few per cent of the register: the controller and his affiliates hold 92.98% on the IDX aggregate measure [S3] and the register figure of 43.21% counts affiliates as public [S5]. The only regime flag the lens applies is HSC status, worth 0.05 of closing share; the free-float deadline is not triggered because the exchange registry measures the float above the minimum (a registry fact, the Director to reconcile), so no second flag is used. The base regime closes part of the log gap in twelve months and the bear regime closes 80%, which is why the target sits between the price and the value rather than at value; the target is a probability-weighted mean across the regime paths, not the modal path [S3, S6].
